sections.heading: What Usually Causes a Sewer Backup
body: Most sewer backups come down to a short list of causes. Here is what we look for.

items.title: A clog in the line
items.text: Grease, wipes, something flushed that shouldn't have been. Often it can be cleared, and we'll tell you if clearing is all it needs.

items.title: Roots in the line
items.text: Tree roots find a small gap in an older line and grow into it. Clearing helps for a while. If the line is damaged, we'll tell you what a lasting fix looks like.

items.title: A collapsed or broken section
items.text: An old line can crack, sag or collapse. Water has nowhere to go, and clearing won't hold. This is when replacing a section, or the line, comes up.

items.title: No cleanout
items.text: A cleanout is the access point that lets a line be cleared. Without one, every job is harder, and adding one can make the next backup easier to deal with.

tail: Which one you have decides everything that follows, so we name it before we talk about the job.

sections.quote: Jaime and his crew were practically immediate in their response to my sewer line needing to be cleared and partially replaced. They were friendly, completely professional, and what I appreciated most was their excellent communication and keeping me apprised of the work and my options every step of the way.
sections.name: Jay P.

sections.heading: Clear It, Repair It or Replace It?
body: Clearing a line is the smaller job and replacing it is the bigger one. You should hear which one the problem calls for, and why, before you hear a price.
A clog is a clearing. A line that has cracked, sagged or collapsed won't stay clear, so replacing the damaged section, or the line, is the honest answer.
Either way, we tell you what we found and what we'd do, and you decide.

sections.quote: they were incredibly nice & respectful about everything the entire time. they talked to me & my husband about what was going on, explained what they would be doing. … they even managed to put back together our concrete patio to the best of their abilities, after it had to be broken up to get underneath for the pipe.
sections.name: Katherine B.

sections.heading: When the Line Runs Under Your Patio or Driveway
body: Some sewer lines run under concrete, a driveway or a patio. If reaching the line means opening one up, you'll hear that before we start, not after.
Tell us what's above the line when you call: a patio, a tree, a flowerbed. All of it changes the job, and we'd rather plan for it than be surprised.

sections.heading: While You Wait for Us
body: Stop running water into the drains. That means the washer, the dishwasher and the showers. More water has nowhere to go, and the backup gets worse.
If you can, note which drains are backing up and when it started. It helps us find the line quickly.

items.q: How do I know it's the sewer line and not just a drain?
items.a: If one sink drains slowly, it's usually that drain. If the lowest drain in the house backs up, or several fixtures gurgle or back up together, the main sewer line is the likely cause. Call and describe it, and we'll tell you what we think.

items.q: Can the line be cleared, or does it have to be replaced?
items.a: It depends on what's wrong. A clog can be cleared. A broken or collapsed section can't. We find which it is, and show you, before we talk about replacing anything.

items.q: Will you dig up my yard?
items.a: Not unless the job calls for it. If it does, you'll hear where and why before we start.

items.q: Can a cleanout be added to my line?
items.a: Often, yes. A cleanout makes the line easier to clear next time. Ask when you call and we'll tell you if it makes sense on your line.

items.q: How long will a sewer job take?
items.a: It depends on the line, what's wrong and what's above it. We'll give you a realistic idea once we've seen it, not a guess over the phone.

sections.heading: Signs a Water Heater Is Done
body: Heaters rarely quit without warning. Here is what the warning looks like.

items.title: No hot water at all
items.text: Sometimes it's a small part, sometimes it's the tank itself. We check, and we tell you which, before anyone talks about replacing it.

items.title: Water around the base
items.text: A leak at the bottom of the tank usually means the tank has failed, and a repair won't fix that. We'll show you where it's coming from.

items.title: Rusty or cloudy hot water
items.text: Rust in the hot water can point to a tank wearing out. We'll tell you what we see and what it means.

items.title: Rumbling or popping
items.text: Sediment builds up in the bottom of a tank over time. Sometimes it's a maintenance issue and sometimes a sign the tank is tired.

items.title: Repairs that keep coming
items.text: A heater that has needed fix after fix is telling you something. We'll tell you where we think yours stands.

tail: Every one of these starts with finding out what's actually wrong.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace?
body: Here's the question that costs you the most. A repair on a heater near the end of its life can be money spent twice.
If the problem is a small part and the tank is sound, repair is the answer. If the tank has failed, or repairs keep coming, replacement is the honest one.
We'll tell you which side you're on and why, and the decision stays yours.

body: A water heater has a way of going out right before something important. Call, and tell us when it went out and whether water is leaking.
We'll tell you on the phone when we can come, and what to do until then.

items.q: Should I repair or replace my water heater?
items.a: It depends on what failed. A small part on a sound tank can be repaired. A leaking tank can't. We find the cause, tell you which it is and why, and you decide.

items.q: Do you repair water heaters too?
items.a: Yes. Repair comes first when repair makes sense.

items.q: What should I do if my water heater is leaking?
items.a: Shut off the water supply to the heater, and the power or gas if you can reach them safely, then call us. Don't wait for it to drain on its own.

items.q: Will you tell me the price before you start?
items.a: Yes. You hear your options and the price before the work begins.
We'll tell you once we've seen the heater. Some jobs are simple and others involve old connections, and a guess over the phone isn't worth much.
